sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows a herniated bowel loop in the left groin. Note the close relationship of the hernia to the femoral vessels at the level of the symphysis pubis, characteristic of a femoral hernia.

sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-05

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows a left abdominal spigelian hernia with multiple dilated loops of small bowel , compatible with small bowel obstruction.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-06

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial NECT shows a large lumbar hernia in the right flank containing a portion of the right kidney .
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-07

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Coronal CECT shows a large lumbar hernia containing colon , small bowel , as well as a portion of the right hepatic lobe . Lumbar hernias are often secondary to prior surgical incisions and are particularly common after renal surgeries.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-08

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Sagittal CECT shows an umbilical hernia containing ascites in a patient with cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-09

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows an enterocutaneous fistula with enteric contrast directly extending from the small bowel into the anterior abdominal wall .
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-10

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows a loop of small bowel lying between the obturator externus and pectineus muscles, compatible with an obturator hernia.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-11

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT in a trauma patient shows disruption of the musculofascial plane near the insertion into the iliac crest and thoracolumbar fascia. Note the presence of adjacent subcutaneous hematoma. The spleen was also lacerated (not shown). These findings are compatible with a traumatic hernia.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-12

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial T1 MR shows a large mass with fat signal extending through the inguinal canal into the left scrotum. This was found to be a spermatic cord liposarcoma at resection.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-13

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Sagittal US in the same patient shows that the mass is very echogenic as a result of its fatty component, a fairly common appearance for these lesions, and extends down to just above the testicle .
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-14

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows a loculated fluid collection in the subcutaneous tissue adjacent to the site of incisional hernia repair (abdominal wall abscess).
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-10

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows a partly calcified mass in the abdominal wall adjacent to a descending colostomy (metastatic colonic carcinoma).
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-11

CORE_EVIDENCE_FILE_BEGIN
CORE_EVIDENCE_STATUS: USED
CORE_SOURCE_BASIS: Core Radiology: A Visual Approach to Diagnostic Imaging, 2nd ed.; Gastrointestinal Imaging, Small Bowel, “Obstruction due to external hernia,” pp. 200–201.
CORE_FACTS_USED:

* External hernias are the second most common cause of small bowel obstruction; approximately 75% occur in the groin, with most being inguinal.
* Indirect inguinal hernia neck is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; direct inguinal hernia neck is medial and protrudes through Hesselbach triangle.
* Incarceration means a hernia cannot be reduced; strangulation means ischemia from vascular compromise.
* Obturator hernia places bowel between the pectineus and obturator muscles.
* Femoral hernia enters the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament and tends to compress the adjacent femoral vein.
* Spigelian hernia occurs at the semilunar line.
* Richter hernia involves only the antimesenteric portion of bowel wall and is more likely to strangulate than obstruct.
CORE_DERIVED_CARDS:
* PRIMARY UNKNOWN and Differential Drill cards involving inguinal, femoral, obturator, and spigelian hernias.
* Definition cards for incarceration, strangulation, and Richter hernia.
* Mechanism card: “Why can a Richter hernia strangulate without causing bowel obstruction?”
* Epidemiology card: “What proportion of external hernias occur in the groin according to Core Radiology?”
* High-Yield cards distinguishing direct/indirect inguinal and femoral/inguinal hernias.
CORE_LIMITATIONS:
* Core coverage used here is concentrated in GI pp. 200–201 and is narrower than the fused RadPrimer/STATdx abdominal-wall hernia package; lumbar, traumatic, umbilical, fistula, liposarcoma, abscess, and abdominal-wall metastasis details were derived from the fused article package rather than Core.
CORE_EVIDENCE_FILE_END
